children: Foreign investors sold Asian bonds in August for the first time in five months, as a global bond selloff and expectations of further monetary policy tightening in major economies curbed appetite for regional debt.

Foreigners divested a net $457 million of bonds in South Korea, Malaysia, India, Indonesia and Thailand, logging their first monthly net sales since March, data from regulators and bond market associations showed.
Bond markets from the US to Germany and Japan came under pressure during the month, with rising government debt and inflation concerns pushing long-term borrowing costs to multi-decade highs.

The European Central Bank raised rates to 2.50% from 2.25% last week, while the Federal Reserve lifted borrowing costs by 25 basis points on Wednesday to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%, as policymakers sought to contain inflation driven by higher energy costs linked to the Iran war.

Analysts said expectations that major central banks would keep policy restrictive for longer, along with concerns about increasing government bond supply in some developed markets, prompted investors to reduce exposure to emerging-market debt.
South Korea recorded the largest outflow, with foreign investors selling about $5.4 billion of bonds after a four-month buying streak.

"This likely reflects some unwinding of positions accumulated ahead of WGBI inclusion, which had driven persistent inflows throughout the year," said Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at ANZ, referring to the FTSE World Government Bond Index.
Thai bonds saw a third straight month of foreign outflows, with investors selling a net $77 million. Foreigners sold $232 million of Indian bonds after two consecutive months of net purchases.
Elsewhere, foreign investors bought $3.95 billion of Malaysian bonds and $1.3 billion of Indonesian debt.
The inflows suggested investors remained selective, favouring markets that offer relatively attractive yields and have stable domestic fundamentals.
